ResearchDossier.topic: one picture made Christmas trees mainstream
ResearchDossier.summary: The Brotherhood of Blackheads put up holiday trees in their guild houses in Reval (Tallinn) and Riga in 1441, 1442, 1510 and 1514. In 1848 The Illustrated London News showed Queen Victoria and Prince Albert's family around a decorated tree at Windsor; within ten years the tradition was widespread in middle and upper-class British homes. In 1850 Godey's Lady's Book copied the picture exactly, except for removing the Queen's tiara and Prince Albert's moustache.
ResearchDossier.angle: A royal photo-op that went viral twice.

Script.headline: One Picture Made Christmas Trees
Script.cta: Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.

lines.text: Christmas trees went mainstream because of one picture.
Decorated trees go back centuries. Guilds in Tallinn and Riga put them up in the 1400s.
But then, in 1848, a London newspaper printed this.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, with their children, around a decorated tree at Windsor Castle.
In fewer than ten years, middle and upper-class homes across Britain were doing the same.
Two years later, an American magazine printed the exact same picture.
With two changes. They erased the Queen's tiara, and Prince Albert's moustache.
Suddenly, it wasn't the royal family. It could have been any family.

PublishCopy.title: One picture made Christmas trees mainstream
PublishCopy.description:
Christmas trees went mainstream because of one picture.
In 1848, The Illustrated London News printed Queen Victoria and Prince Albert's family around a decorated tree at Windsor. Within ten years, homes across Britain copied it. Two years later, an American magazine reprinted it, but erased the Queen's tiara and Albert's moustache.
